beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Egregopathy asks why replacing harmful leaders can leave an institution's behavior unchanged.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its proposed concept describes harm protected by roles, targets, and selective information.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book treats this as institutional design, not a psychiatric diagnosis.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It asks whether moral concern can change objectives when correction costs something.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Take its opening image of a company poisoning a river.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Imagine its managers seeing revenue reports while a downstream household loses usable water.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Different departments defend production, legal compliance, and reputation through separate measures.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: An apology changes the message, while the discharge continues unchanged.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book's test is whether evidence of harm can constrain that process.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The historical chapters trace a disturbing pattern across very different forms of organized power.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book later challenges the evidence it selected to make that pattern persuasive.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Accurate examples can mislead when contrary examples remain outside the frame.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Institutions also create public health, shared resources, scientific knowledge, and constraints on powerful actors.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That counterhistory tests whether the proposed concept explains more than its dramatic language suggests.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers gain two investigations: how institutions resist correction, and how arguments recruit belief.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The Moral Turing Test asks what an institution's apology makes impossible afterward.
